report:
**Conclusion: Supported, but with important qualifiers.** In people with chronic inflammatory diseases, anti-cytokine drugs show a **modest antidepressant effect**, not a robust stand-alone depression treatment. The strongest evidence is a *Molecular Psychiatry* systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs in chronic inflammatory conditions where depression was a secondary outcome: anti-cytokine treatment beat placebo (SMD ≈ 0.40, 95% CI 0.22–0.59); anti-TNF agents were most studied (SMD ≈ 0.33), and adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab and tocilizumab each improved depressive symptoms. Crucially, response tracked **baseline depressive severity** and was **not explained by improvement in the physical illness**, suggesting a specific mood effect rather than only “feeling better because disease improved.” https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5794896/

A broader JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis likewise found anti-inflammatory treatments (NSAIDs and cytokine inhibitors) reduced depressive symptoms versus placebo, supporting a real but moderate signal. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1916904

However, in primary treatment-resistant depression, infliximab was **not generally effective**; benefit appeared mainly in patients with high baseline inflammation (e.g., elevated hs-CRP). This implies the effect is context- and biomarker-dependent, not universal. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/1356541

Caveats: many trials measured depression secondarily, samples had inflammatory disease, effects are modest, heterogeneity and safety/immunosuppression matter. So the claim is **true for symptom reduction in chronic inflammatory conditions**, especially with higher baseline inflammation/severe symptoms, but should not be read as proof that anti-cytokine drugs are general antidepressants. https://www.nature.com/articles/mp2016167
